title: Ciannait finds the third stone standing
summary: Ciannait, driving her household's beasts down to the autumn stubble, finds a squared pillar newly standing on the rise by the drove-road where no stone had stood the year before, and reads aloud, alone but for a boy of her own kin, the four words cut low on its face and the whole saying beneath them.

title: The rise takes the name Achadh a' Chalbh
summary: The hearths that gather to look at the new pillar begin to call the rise Achadh a' Chalbh, a name that settles into use before any household troubles to remember which mouth first gave it.

title: The whole saying said standing for the first time
summary: At a gathering of some thirty households kept at Achadh a' Chalbh on Oidhche an Dealanaich, an old woman of a neighbouring valley says the sayings of all three stones together before a crowd, and ties the third saying to Aithris a' Chruthachaidh's grass-people and the island as their only root.

title: The gathering at the column kept a second year, and a third
summary: More households come to keep the dark of the year at Achadh a' Chalbh than came the winter before, and the ground about the pillar's foot begins to wear bare under their standing, so that within Ciannait's own lifetime the column becomes the one gathering-ground of that whole stretch of country.

title: A market grows up at the column's gatherings
summary: Traders begin setting hides, salt and wool out on cloths spread over the trampled ground at Achadh a' Chalbh on the two days a year the crowds are greatest, taking their goods up again each evening, for no one yet thinks to leave anything standing there overnight but the stone.

title: A boy of the keeper's hearth hears of the third stone
summary: At Tobar dhìreach a fire-bearer carries the first word of the pillar and its saying to the keeper's own hearth, and a boy not yet six turns gual teine in his fingers as he listens, asking his mother whether the coal and the stone's saying come from the one place.

title: The saying carried to the northern shore
summary: A woman of the northern shore, come south to trade hides for salt at one of Achadh a' Chalbh's market days, hears the whole saying said at the stone and carries it home the length of the island, telling it first at her own hearth to a household that keeps no stone and no gathering-ground of its own.

title: A north-western shepherd answers a trader with the saying
summary: A shepherd of the far north-western moor, asked by a passing trader what his own people hold of where they came from, answers with the third stone's four words, though he has never walked south to hear them said at Achadh a' Chalbh himself.

title: Ciannait says the saying to her children by her own fire
summary: In the last winter of her life, her joints too cold-bitten for the walk to Achadh a' Chalbh, Ciannait says the third stone's saying once more to her children at her own hearth, tying it plainly to Aithris a' Chruthachaidh of the grass-people grown from the island's own ground.

title: Ciannait dies at her own hearth
summary: Ciannait dies in her one and seventieth year at the hearth where she was born, and is buried, as her own kin have always been buried, without any coal of the vein given her in the ground, that custom never having reached so far south-west in her lifetime.

title: Ciannait's children keep the walk to the column after her
summary: Ciannait's children take up the walk to Achadh a' Chalbh in her stead, not every year but often enough that the fire at the pillar's foot never goes long unlit in their own generation, and the saying she gave them at her hearth goes on being said by mouths that never stood at the stone itself.
